questions.prompt: Two variables point to the same list and one appends an item. What should you expect?
options: Both names can observe the mutation
questions.answer: Both names can observe the mutation
questions.explanation: Python variables are names bound to objects. Lists are mutable, so mutating through one reference is visible through another reference to the same object.

concept_panel.title: Variables and References
concept_panel.explanation: Python variables are names bound to objects. Lists are mutable, so mutating through one reference is visible through another reference to the same object.
concept_panel.practical_example: a = []; b = a; b.append(1) leaves a as [1].
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you understand Python references rather than assuming assignment copies data.

questions.prompt: Which value is safest as a dictionary key?
questions.explanation: Dictionary keys must be hashable. Immutable tuples containing hashable values can be keys; mutable lists, dictionaries, and sets cannot.

concept_panel.title: Mutable vs Immutable
concept_panel.explanation: Dictionary keys must be hashable. Immutable tuples containing hashable values can be keys; mutable lists, dictionaries, and sets cannot.
concept_panel.practical_example: Use ('region', 'month') as a composite key for cached KPI results.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you understand mutability and hashing constraints.

questions.prompt: You repeatedly test whether user IDs were already seen. Which collection fits best?
questions.explanation: Sets provide average O(1) membership checks and model uniqueness. Lists preserve order but membership is O(n).

concept_panel.title: Lists, Tuples, Sets, Dictionaries
concept_panel.explanation: Sets provide average O(1) membership checks and model uniqueness. Lists preserve order but membership is O(n).
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you choose data structures by access pattern.

questions.prompt: A list contains one million IDs. What is the cost of `target in ids`?
questions.explanation: List membership scans until it finds the item or reaches the end, so it is linear. Dict and set membership are average O(1).

concept_panel.title: Time Complexity of Common Operations
concept_panel.explanation: List membership scans until it finds the item or reaches the end, so it is linear. Dict and set membership are average O(1).
concept_panel.practical_example: Convert a list to a set before many membership checks.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you can reason about Python performance without guessing.

questions.prompt: Which check is most Pythonic for a list that may be empty?
questions.explanation: Empty containers are falsy and non-empty containers are truthy. Use `if items:` when you only care whether a collection has content.

concept_panel.title: Truthiness
concept_panel.explanation: Empty containers are falsy and non-empty containers are truthy. Use `if items:` when you only care whether a collection has content.
concept_panel.practical_example: Return early with `if not rows:` when a query returns no records.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you know idiomatic Python boolean behavior.

questions.prompt: How should you usually check whether a variable is None?
questions.explanation: `is` checks identity and None is a singleton, so `is None` is the idiomatic check. `==` delegates to equality logic and may be overloaded.

concept_panel.title: is vs ==
concept_panel.explanation: `is` checks identity and None is a singleton, so `is None` is the idiomatic check. `==` delegates to equality logic and may be overloaded.
concept_panel.practical_example: Use `if user is None:` after a repository lookup.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you separate identity from equality.

questions.prompt: Which operation is average O(1) in a dictionary?
questions.explanation: Dictionaries are hash tables optimized for key lookup, insertion, and deletion on average. Searching values still requires scanning.

concept_panel.title: Dictionary Operations
concept_panel.explanation: Dictionaries are hash tables optimized for key lookup, insertion, and deletion on average. Searching values still requires scanning.
concept_panel.practical_example: settings['DATABASE_URL'] is a direct key lookup.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you understand common dictionary operation costs.

questions.prompt: Why might an interview answer choose a tuple over a list?
questions.explanation: Tuples communicate fixed-size immutable records. They can also be hashable if their elements are hashable.

concept_panel.title: Tuple Use Cases
concept_panel.explanation: Tuples communicate fixed-size immutable records. They can also be hashable if their elements are hashable.
concept_panel.practical_example: Represent a coordinate as (x, y) when it should not be mutated.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you understand semantic collection choice.

questions.prompt: A deduplication step should keep only unique customer IDs. What structure fits?
questions.explanation: Sets represent uniqueness and support fast membership checks. They do not preserve duplicates.

concept_panel.title: Set Semantics
concept_panel.explanation: Sets represent uniqueness and support fast membership checks. They do not preserve duplicates.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you can model uniqueness directly.

questions.prompt: Why is Python often chosen for backend and AI product work?
options: Fast development with strong ecosystem support
It is always faster than Java
It removes the need for tests
questions.answer: Fast development with strong ecosystem support
questions.explanation: Python is productive, readable, and has excellent web, data, ML, and automation libraries. The trade-off is runtime performance and dynamic typing risks that require tests and discipline.

concept_panel.title: Why Python
concept_panel.explanation: Python is productive, readable, and has excellent web, data, ML, and automation libraries. The trade-off is runtime performance and dynamic typing risks that require tests and discipline.
concept_panel.practical_example: FastAPI plus pandas/scikit-learn can ship an analytics API quickly.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you can explain pragmatic language trade-offs.

questions.prompt: What is a fair Python-vs-Java trade-off?
options: Python is faster to iterate; Java often offers stronger static typing and JVM performance
Python always beats Java at scale
questions.answer: Python is faster to iterate; Java often offers stronger static typing and JVM performance
questions.explanation: Python and Java solve overlapping problems with different trade-offs. Java often offers stronger compile-time guarantees; Python often wins in iteration speed and AI/data ecosystems.

concept_panel.title: Why Not Java
concept_panel.explanation: Python and Java solve overlapping problems with different trade-offs. Java often offers stronger compile-time guarantees; Python often wins in iteration speed and AI/data ecosystems.
concept_panel.practical_example: Use Python for ML-heavy services; use Java when a team values JVM tooling and static contracts.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you can compare languages without shallow absolutes.

questions.prompt: What makes Python's object model different from many beginner mental models?
options: Names bind to objects rather than variables storing raw values
questions.answer: Names bind to objects rather than variables storing raw values
questions.explanation: Everything is an object, and assignment binds a name to an object. Understanding that model explains mutability, identity, default argument bugs, and object sharing.

concept_panel.title: What Makes Python Different
concept_panel.explanation: Everything is an object, and assignment binds a name to an object. Understanding that model explains mutability, identity, default argument bugs, and object sharing.
concept_panel.practical_example: `a = b` binds a second name to the same object, not a deep copy.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you understand Python fundamentals deeply enough to avoid subtle bugs.

coding_challenges.title: EPAM Python Core status classifier
coding_challenges.instructions: Implement classify_status_code(code: int) -> str. Return success for 200-299, redirect for 300-399, client_error for 400-499, server_error for 500-599, and unknown otherwise.
coding_challenges.explanation: The challenge reinforces deterministic branching, status-code categories, and local test execution.
